extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, counsel in USPTO disciplinary/reciprocal-discipline matters, and USPTO/OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 based on a state bar's disciplinary adjudication (including assessing Selling v. Radford factors, procedural requirements, and appropriate sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for imposing reciprocal discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The USPTO Director shall consider the record and shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: …” (text of 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) excerpted in the order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a presumption in favor of imposing identical reciprocal discipline; the Director’s default course is to impose the same discipline unless the practitioner meets the narrow exceptions set forth in the regulation (see the Selling factors below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford factors (grounds to avoid reciprocal discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may prevent imposition of reciprocal discipline by showing (1) a want of due process; (2) an infirmity of proof of the misconduct; or (3) that grave injustice would result from imposition of reciprocal discipline (as articulated under Selling v. Radford and mirrored in 37 C.F.R. § 11.24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three Selling factors are the core exceptions to the presumption of reciprocal discipline; the practitioner must raise a genuine issue of material fact as to at least one by clear and convincing evidence. The regulation also includes an explicit fourth clause addressing arguments that the practitioner was not publicly disciplined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process deprivation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard in a meaningful time and manner. Typical indicia: receipt of notice of charges, ability to participate in hearings, opportunity to present evidence and witnesses, to testify, to cross-examine opposing witnesses, to be represented by counsel, and to make arguments. Mere disagreement with evidentiary rulings or outcome does not establish deprivation of due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet this standard the respondent must show, by clear and convincing evidence, that the state proceeding’s proof was so deficient that the USPTO could not accept the result. Courts and the USPTO give deference to trier-of-fact credibility determinations; mere disagreement with findings or credibility does not satisfy this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grave-injustice inquiry asks whether the sanction is so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that imposing the same discipline would be unfair. Consideration may include mitigating factors and the range of appropriate sanctions; if the state sanction is within a reasonable range, reciprocal imposition is generally not a grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof (practitioner’s burden: clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that a genuine issue of material fact exists as to one of the Selling/§11.24 exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal/USPTO precedent consistently treats this showing as narrow and difficult to make; the practitioner bears the burden and must produce evidence sufficient to raise a genuine material factual dispute under a high standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-de novo nature of reciprocal-discipline proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reciprocal disciplinary proceedings are not in any sense de novo proceedings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO Director is not sitting as a court of review to find errors in the state tribunal’s proceedings. Reciprocal proceedings are not a vehicle to retry the original disciplinary matter, correct garden‑variety errors, or relitigate factual or credibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default judgments and deemed admissions can support discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO precedent recognizes that a disbarment or other sanction based on a state default judgment (and the resulting deemed admissions) can be a sufficient basis for reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that default judgments are inherently insufficient to support discipline are rejected by USPTO decisions; prior USPTO proceedings have imposed exclusions where the underlying state disbarment followed default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements/examples of procedural due-process protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific protections showing due process: notice of charges, ability to respond to allegations, opportunity to testify at length in own defense, present witnesses and evidence, cross‑examine witnesses, be represented by counsel, and make arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a due-process claim, the Director examines the record to confirm these procedural opportunities existed; documentary proof (e.g., notices, filings, hearing transcripts, counsel participation) is strong evidence that due process was afforded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors for discipline (ABA Standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Maryland court cited aggravating factors from the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions: dishonest or selfish motive; a pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding; submission of false evidence/false statements/deceptive practices during the proceeding; refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct; and substantial experience in the practice of law. The only mitigating factor found was absence of prior discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors inform whether the state sanction is appropriate and are relevant to the grave‑injustice analysis; aggravating factors weigh toward more severe discipline, while mitigating factors may reduce severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural mechanics of USPTO reciprocal discipline (notice, response timeline, motions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice and Order pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 is served (email/certified mail); respondent has an opportunity to file a response (the Notice provided 40 days in this case); the Director may grant limited extensions and set briefing schedules; parties may file motions but substantive arguments must be timely and properly presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural compliance (timely filing of response, adherence to briefing schedule, proper use of motions) matters; failing to respond or repeatedly seeking dilatory relief can be considered in the record and may undermine a respondent’s positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and administrative consequences upon imposition of reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Where reciprocal discipline is appropriate the Order directs outcomes such as exclusion from practice before the USPTO (in patent, trademark, and other non‑patent matters), publication of a notice materially consistent with the order in the Official Gazette, notice to state disciplinary agencies and courts, requirements to comply with duties under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58, dissociation from USPTO customer numbers, and prohibition on obtaining or being added to a Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order specifies both the substantive sanction (exclusion/disbarment) and collateral administrative steps the USPTO will take to effect and publicize the discipline; these are standard follow-on actions after a reciprocal discipline determination.
